subject: Physics
description: Motion in two dimensions with interactive trajectory whiteboard
summary:
This lesson covered the foundational principles of two-dimensional kinematics, focusing on the independence of horizontal and vertical motion. Students learned to break initial velocity vectors into orthogonal components using trigonometric functions: vx = v * cos(θ) along the horizontal axis and vy = v * sin(θ) along the vertical axis.

By analyzing trajectory curves on the interactive whiteboard, the class explored how gravity acts solely along the vertical axis (ay = -g) while horizontal velocity remains constant in the absence of air resistance (ax = 0). Combining these independent parametric equations yields the classic parabolic trajectory, allowing students to systematically plot trajectories, determine peak height, and calculate projectile range.
revisionQuestions: What are the mathematical formulas used to decompose an initial velocity vector v at launch angle θ into horizontal and vertical components?
A student claims that the acceleration of a projectile is zero at its maximum height because vy = 0. Explain why this reasoning is incorrect.

A projectile is launched from ground level with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. What is its maximum height? (Hint: Use v_0y = 20 * sin(30°) = 10 m/s and vy^2 = v_0y^2 - 2gΔy with g = 9.8 m/s²; Δy ≈ 5.1 m)
